extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, narratologists, and advanced creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and analytic criteria for studying narrative voice (author/narrator functions), the narratee/implied reader relation, and the formal effects of commentary vs. story (e.g., iterative technique, focalization, anachrony). Useful for close-reading or for guiding creative decisions about narration in the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-narrative functions of the author-narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses to the reader, organization of the narrative by means of advance notices and recalls, indications of source, memory-elicited attestations (and related manifestations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These functions are not watertight compartments and often overlap; they serve as vehicles of realistic motivation or justification. Examples include advance notices/prolepses and recalls, indications of source, memory attestations; the text warns these may be mixed and vary in emphasis across authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative degree of authorial intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount and visibility of the author's or narrator's interventions in the narrative (e.g., Balzac 'intervenes' more than Flaubert; Fielding addresses the reader more often than Mme. de La Fayette).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervention cannot be completely avoided and is a matter of emphasis and relative weight; comparisons (Balzac vs Flaubert, Fielding vs Mme. de La Fayette, Cooper/Mann vs Hemingway) illustrate a spectrum rather than discrete types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological function and its (quasi-)monopoly by the narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's role as the principal vehicle of ideological, psychological, historical, aesthetic, metaphysical commentary—often a quasi-monopoly but not necessarily obligatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike other extra-narrative functions, ideological commentary need not revert to the narrator in every work; some novelists (Dostoevski, Tolstoy, Mann, Malraux) transfer commentary to characters, while Proust largely entrusts it to his narrator. Evaluate who carries ideological discourse and how deliberately that choice is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as spokesmen vs objects provoking thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether characters serve as authorized interlocutors/spokesmen of ideas or are observed as objects that provoke thought in the narrator/reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proustian model: characters (Swann, Saint-Loup, Charlus, Bergotte, Vinteuil, Elstir) are objects of observation rather than custodians of truth; their errors and failures instruct more than their opinions. Assess whether characters function as expository mouthpieces or as material that elicits commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invasion of narrative by commentary (essayization of the novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the story is interrupted or permeated by commentary, turning narrative toward essay, commentary, or didactic discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such invasion can change novelistic form (e.g., Proust's narrative is 'not completely a novel any more'), affecting closure and potentially inaugurating modern literature. Measure how commentary transforms narrative balance and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diegetic level of the narratee (intradiegetic vs extradiegetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the intended receiver within the narrating situation is situated on the same diegetic level as the narrator (intradiegetic) or on a higher/extradiegetic level (extradiegetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An intradiegetic narratee is a fictional addressee (e.g., Renoncourt, Pinot) distinct from the real reader; an extradiegetic narratee can merge with the implied reader and the real reader can identify with them. This choice affects address marks, distance, and possible reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of the receiving instance and reader identification
rubrics_metrics.description: How overt or silent the narratee's presence is in the text; greater transparency/silence makes substitution/identification by the real reader easier and more irresistible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the receiving instance is interposed (intradiegetic narratee), readers remain at a distance. If it is transparent (ex. extradiegetic implicit addressee), real readers more readily insert themselves as the implied narratee. Use this to evaluate reader engagement strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address and the implied reader's liberty to reinterpret
rubrics_metrics.description: The text's invitation to the reader to 'guess,' interpret, and translate the work into his own terms; the author's duty to grant the reader liberty of reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proustian injunction: 'the author must leave the reader all possible liberty.' Assess how a narrative anticipates and requires active reader interpretation and how much freedom the author affords for idiosyncratic readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader as co-creator (narrative as instrument)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the reader contributes to the making of the text (reader-as-producer rather than consumer), rewriting or completing the work from within.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models and metaphors (Pierre Menard rewriting Quixote) show the real author can be he who hears; analyze techniques that make reading generative (ambiguity, partial disclosure, iterative structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness vs closure (completion and the 'sense of unfulfillment')
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work tends toward closure and final message or maintains an open, indefinite, unfinished quality that resists neat synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette argues for restoring works like Proust to 'their sense of unfulfillment' and warns against forcing unity/coherence; evaluate whether completions are retrospective illusions and whether narrative contingency is acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analytic categories as provisional tools (avoid hypostatizing into canon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts and technical categories (prolepses, analepses, iterative, focalizations, metadiegetic, pseudo-diegetic) are instruments of discovery, not fixed Canons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should treat such terminology as provisional, empirical tools that may become outmoded; avoid turning the descriptive 'grid' into an incarcerating set of rules or a prescriptive Canon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical preference for deviance, originality, and 'writerly' features
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency (and permissible critical stance) to privilege deviant, original, or 'writerly' aspects of a text—features that make readers producers rather than passive consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author acknowledges this bias: analysts often emphasize transgressive or nascent features (iterativity, pseudo-diegetic modes). Recognize this as a legitimate, though partial, critical posture and make it explicit when it informs analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal features to attend to (iterative, pseudo-diegetic, anachronies, multiple focalizations, metadiegetic eliminations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific narratological phenomena the analyst should notice: iterative narrative, pseudo-diegetic formations, anachronies (anachrony), multiple focalizations, the presence or elimination of the metadiegetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features can be diagnostic of an author's innovations (e.g., Proust): assess their presence, functions, and interactions (for instance, between disappearance of summary and emergence of iterative). The book gives examples and argues these deserve further investigation rather than being dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological humility and acceptance of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit recognition that categories chosen are imperfect, ephemeral, and the product of tradeoffs; the critic must accept decay and revision of theoretical objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette advises self-criticism: the proliferation of concepts may annoy readers; one should expect many propositions to be revised. This invites critics to use tools empirically and to remain open to debate and revision.
